lesson.title: Forwarding: A Router's Per Packet Decision
lesson.summary: Forwarding is the process by which a router examines an arriving packet's destination address, looks it up in its forwarding table, and sends the packet out toward the correct next hop, repeated independently for every packet that passes through.
lesson.body:
Getting a packet from a source to a destination across a network of routers is not one decision, it is many small, repeated decisions, one made independently at every router the packet happens to pass through. Each of those individual decisions, made by a single router about a single packet, is what forwarding refers to. It is worth separating this from the broader, ongoing job of building and maintaining a router's knowledge of the network, usually called routing, which runs continuously in the background through protocols and configuration. Forwarding is the fast, repeated, per packet action that draws on whatever that background process has already worked out.

When a packet arrives at a router, the router reads the destination address out of the packet's header and looks it up against its forwarding table, a set of entries that map address prefixes to a next hop, meaning either another router further along the path or a directly connected destination, along with the outgoing interface to use. Having found a match, the router decrements the packet's time to live, which, as the traceroute chapter described, is exactly the field that eventually triggers an ICMP time exceeded message if it reaches zero. The router then wraps the packet in a new link layer frame addressed to that next hop, which on a typical local network means resolving the next hop's MAC address through ARP or NDP first, and sends it out the chosen interface.

Picture a packet destined for 8.8.8.8 arriving at a home router. That router's forwarding table is simple, typically just a default route, written as 0.0.0.0/0, pointing to its internet provider's next hop address. The packet does not match anything more specific, so the router falls back to that default entry, decrements the time to live, and forwards the packet out its internet facing interface toward the provider. That provider's own router repeats the exact same process using its own, considerably larger forwarding table, and so does every router after it, each one making its own independent forwarding decision, until the packet finally reaches a router that knows how to deliver it directly to its destination. This is precisely what traceroute reveals when it maps out a path: each hop it lists is one router's forwarding decision, captured one at a time by exploiting how each of those routers handles an expiring time to live.

Forwarding tables are not always as tidy as a single default route. A router can easily hold several entries that all technically match the same destination address, an aggregate route alongside a more specific one learned separately, or a specific customer route sitting alongside a broad default. When more than one entry matches, the router needs a consistent rule for choosing between them, which is exactly the problem the next chapter addresses.
